o: It is part of the panniculus carnosus

Platysma is part of the panniculus carnosus, lying in the superficial fascia, and is supplied by VII.
It is a muscle of facial expression that has spread into the neck.
It covers the external and anterior jugular veins

Platysma covers the external and anterior jugular veins and may help to relieve pressure on them.
These veins lie deep to it in the superficial fascia.
It is supplied by the marginal mandibular branch of the facial nerve

Platysma is supplied by the cervical branch of VII, with proprioception via the transverse cervical nerve.
The marginal mandibular branch supplies the lower lip muscles.
Its lateral border forms zygomaticus minor

The lateral border of platysma forms risorius, attached to the modiolus at the angle of the mouth.
Zygomaticus minor arises from the zygomatic bone region.

questions.s: The superficial part of the submandibular gland (Last's):
o: Its lateral surface is grooved by the facial artery

The facial artery grooves the back of the lateral surface of the superficial part of the gland as it hooks under the mandible.
It must be dealt with when removing the gland. (Last's p. 436)
Its inferior surface is crossed by the facial vein

The inferior (superficial) surface of the gland is crossed by the facial vein and the cervical branch of VII.
The marginal mandibular branch may also cross it if low. (Last's p. 436)
Its medial surface lies mostly against hyoglossus

The medial surface lies mostly against mylohyoid; hyoglossus is overlapped only posteriorly.
The deep part of the gland wraps around the back of mylohyoid onto hyoglossus. (Last's p. 436)
It overlaps the masseter insertion

The superficial part overlaps the front of the medial pterygoid insertion, not the masseter insertion.
Masseter lies on the outer surface of the ramus. (Last's p. 436)

questions.s: The deep part of the gland and its duct (Last's):
o: The lingual nerve lies above the deep part

Between mylohyoid and hyoglossus, the lingual nerve lies above the deep part of the gland, with the duct and XII below.
The submandibular ganglion hangs from the lingual nerve here. (Last's p. 436)
The duct is about 5 cm long

The submandibular duct is about 5 cm long, the same length as the parotid duct.
It runs forward to the sublingual papilla. (Last's p. 436)
The hypoglossal nerve lies above the deep part

XII lies below the deep part of the gland, with the duct.
The lingual nerve is the structure above. (Last's p. 436)
The duct emerges from the deep part of the gland

The duct emerges from the superficial part of the gland near the posterior border of mylohyoid, then runs forward with the deep part.
It is easy to assume it starts in the deep part. (Last's p. 436)
Preganglionic fibres arise in the superior salivary nucleus

Secretomotor fibres start in the superior salivary nucleus, run in the nervus intermedius and chorda tympani (via the lingual nerve), and relay in the submandibular ganglion.
Postganglionic fibres go to the submandibular and sublingual glands. (Last's p. 436)
Sympathetic fibres come from the plexus on the facial artery

Postganglionic sympathetic (vasoconstrictor) fibres reach the gland from the plexus on the facial artery.
They come from the superior cervical ganglion. (Last's p. 436)
Preganglionic fibres run in the lesser petrosal nerve

Preganglionic fibres to the submandibular ganglion run in the nervus intermedius, chorda tympani and lingual nerve. The lesser petrosal nerve carries IX fibres to the otic ganglion for the parotid.
Do not mix up the two salivary pathways. (Last's p. 436)
All secretomotor cell bodies lie in the submandibular ganglion

Last's says a few secretomotor cell bodies lie in small ganglionic masses on the gland itself, not all in the submandibular ganglion.
So some fibres relay in the gland. (Last's p. 436)
It begins near the greater horn of the hyoid

The external carotid begins where the common carotid bifurcates, usually at the level of the upper border of the thyroid cartilage, near the greater horn of the hyoid.
The level varies. (Last's p. 436)
It divides behind the neck of the mandible

The external carotid divides behind the neck of the mandible, within the parotid, into the maxillary and superficial temporal arteries.
These are its terminal branches. (Last's p. 436)
It lies lateral to the internal carotid at its origin

At its origin the external carotid lies medial; the internal carotid is really lateral at its origin.
The names describe territory, not position at the bifurcation. (Last's p. 436)
The IJV lies medial to it at its commencement

At its commencement the internal jugular vein lies lateral to the external carotid, then becomes posterior and deep.
The vein lies outside the arteries. (Last's p. 436)

questions.s: Branches of the external carotid below the parotid:
o: There are six

Before entering the parotid the external carotid gives six branches: three in front (superior thyroid, lingual, facial), two behind (occipital, posterior auricular) and one medial (ascending pharyngeal).
The two terminal branches arise in the gland. (Last's p. 436)
The ascending pharyngeal is the medial branch

The ascending pharyngeal is the only medial branch, running up the pharyngeal wall beside the internal carotid.
It supplies the pharynx, palate and posterior fossa dura. (Last's p. 436)
The occipital artery arises from the front

The occipital artery arises from the back of the external carotid, with the posterior auricular.
The front branches are superior thyroid, lingual and facial. (Last's p. 436)
The facial artery runs along the upper border of the posterior belly of digastric

The occipital and posterior auricular arteries run along the borders of the posterior belly of digastric. The facial artery runs deep to the posterior belly and stylohyoid.
The occipital follows the lower border, the posterior auricular the upper. (Last's p. 436)

questions.s: Separating the external from the internal carotid artery are:
o: The styloid process

The styloid process lies between the external carotid (superficial) and internal carotid (deep).
It is part of the "styloid barrier" between the two arteries. (Last's p. 436)
Stylopharyngeus

Stylopharyngeus passes between the two carotids from the styloid to the pharynx.
It is the only muscle supplied by IX. (Last's p. 436)
The glossopharyngeal nerve

IX accompanies stylopharyngeus between the two arteries; the pharyngeal branch of X also passes between them.
These structures separate the arteries. (Last's p. 436)
The hypoglossal nerve

XII crosses both carotids superficially rather than passing between them.
It lies on the lateral surface of both arteries. (Last's p. 436)
The internal vertebral plexus receives mainly basivertebral veins

Large basivertebral veins draining red marrow from the vertebral bodies are the main tributaries of the internal vertebral venous plexus.
They emerge from the backs of the bodies. (Last's p. 574)
It is a bypass of the diaphragm during raised abdominal pressure

When abdominal pressure rises, blood can bypass the IVC up the valveless vertebral plexus to the SVC. This also allows spread of cancer (for example prostate to spine).
Batson's plexus. (Last's p. 574)
The internal vertebral plexus has valves

The internal vertebral plexus has no valves.
That is why flow can reverse and carry tumour emboli. (Last's p. 574)
The spinal dura fits tightly within the canal

Last's says the cord is narrower than the dura, and the dura narrower than the canal, so the dura does not fit tightly.
The extradural space holds fat and veins. (Last's p. 574)
It is the inner layer of posterior fossa dura continued

The spinal dura is the inner (meningeal) layer of the posterior fossa dura continued through the foramen magnum. The outer periosteal layer stops at the foramen.
So there is no periosteal layer in the spinal dura. (Last's p. 574)
It attaches firmly to the PLL on the axis

The spinal dura attaches firmly to the posterior longitudinal ligament on the axis and to the tectorial membrane.
These are its main upper attachments. (Last's p. 574)
It is firmly attached to the lumbar vertebral bodies

Apart from its upper attachments, the spinal dura is free of bony attachments; it is not firmly attached to the lumbar vertebral bodies.
Only loose fibrous slips tether it. (Last's p. 574)
It ends at L2

The spinal dural sac ends at S2.
The cord ends at about L1/L2. (Last's p. 574)
The filum terminale perforates the theca at S2

The filum terminale pierces the dural sac at S2 and continues to the back of the coccyx.
Its lower part is ensheathed by dura. (Last's p. 574-5)
The lowest denticulation lies at the L1 root

The lowest tooth of the denticulate ligament is at the level of the L1 root.
There are about 21 teeth on each side. (Last's p. 574-5)
The filum terminale ends at the tip of the sacrum

The filum terminale descends to the back of the coccyx, not just to the tip of the sacrum.
It anchors the dural sac. (Last's p. 574-5)
The arachnoid strands are well developed in the anterior midline

The arachnoid strands (subarachnoid trabeculae) are best developed in the posterior midline, forming an incomplete posterior septum.
Anteriorly there is no septum. (Last's p. 574-5)
The spinal subarachnoid space holds about 75 ml of CSF

About half the CSF (about 75 ml) is in the spinal subarachnoid space.
That is why lumbar puncture yields plenty of CSF. (Last's p. 575)
The needle passes supraspinous then interspinous ligaments

A lumbar puncture needle passes the skin, supraspinous and interspinous ligaments, ligamentum flavum, then dura and arachnoid.
A "give" is felt at the ligamentum flavum and again at the dura. (Last's p. 575)
The spinal cord ends at L3 in the adult

The spinal cord ends at about L1 (L1/2 disc) in the adult, not L3.
L3 is its level at birth. (Last's p. 575)
Epidural anaesthetic is injected into the subarachnoid space

Epidural anaesthetic is injected into the extradural space, not the subarachnoid space.
Spinal anaesthetic is injected into the subarachnoid space. (Last's p. 575)
The carotid sinus wall contains baroreceptors

The wall of the carotid sinus contains baroreceptors, supplied by the glossopharyngeal nerve.
It lies at the origin of the internal carotid. (Last's p. 438)
The carotid body lies behind the bifurcation

The carotid body is a small structure behind the carotid bifurcation, supplied by glomic arteries.
It is a chemoreceptor. (Last's p. 438)
The carotid body is supplied by the ascending pharyngeal artery

The carotid body is supplied by glomic arteries from the bifurcation, not by the ascending pharyngeal artery.
Its blood flow is very high for its size. (Last's p. 438)
The carotid body is mainly innervated by the vagus

The carotid body is mainly innervated by the glossopharyngeal nerve (carotid sinus nerve), with lesser contributions from X and sympathetic fibres.
IX is the main afferent nerve. (Last's p. 438)

questions.s: Relations of the cervical internal carotid (Last's):
o: The sympathetic trunk lies behind it outside the sheath

The sympathetic trunk lies behind the internal carotid, outside the carotid sheath, on the prevertebral fascia.
So it is not inside the sheath. (Last's p. 438)
The superior laryngeal nerve crosses obliquely behind it

The superior laryngeal nerve crosses obliquely behind the internal carotid to its medial side and divides there.
XII, by contrast, crosses in front. (Last's p. 438)
It gives several branches in the neck

The internal carotid has no branches in the neck.
That helps identify it at operation. (Last's p. 438)
Its surface marking runs to the tragus

The surface marking of the internal carotid runs up to the head of the mandible. The external carotid line runs to the tragus.
Both start at the bifurcation. (Last's p. 438)
It leaves the posterior compartment of the jugular foramen

The internal jugular vein begins as the jugular bulb in the posterior (largest) compartment of the jugular foramen.
It continues the sigmoid sinus. (Last's p. 438)
Its first tributary is the inferior petrosal sinus

The inferior petrosal sinus joins the internal jugular just below the skull base as its first tributary.
It crosses IX, X and XI to reach the vein. (Last's p. 438)
The thoracic duct crosses behind the right vein at C7

The thoracic duct crosses behind the left internal jugular vein at C7, not the right.
The right lymphatic duct is much smaller. (Last's p. 438)
The inferior root of the ansa curls round its medial border

The inferior root of the ansa cervicalis curls round the lateral border of the internal jugular vein, not the medial border.
It then joins the superior root in front of the vein. (Last's p. 438)

questions.s: Tributaries and surface marking of the IJV:
o: The pharyngeal plexus joins above the facial vein

Last's gives the order of tributaries with the pharyngeal plexus joining above the facial vein.
The facial vein joins near the hyoid. (Last's p. 439)
The middle thyroid is the lowest named tributary

Below the inferior petrosal sinus the tributaries are, in order, pharyngeal, facial, lingual, superior thyroid and middle thyroid. The middle thyroid is the lowest named tributary.
The inferior thyroid veins go to the brachiocephalic. (Last's p. 439)
The surface marking runs from the tragus to the sternal end of the clavicle

The surface marking of the internal jugular vein runs from the ear lobule (not the tragus) to the sternal end of the clavicle.
It lies deep to sternocleidomastoid. (Last's p. 439)
At 45 degrees the jugular pulse is normally seen at the angle of the mandible

With the patient at 45 degrees, the jugular venous pulse is normally seen just above the clavicle, not at the angle of the mandible.
A pulse seen higher indicates raised venous pressure. (Last's p. 439)
The vagus always lies between the IJV and ICA

The vagus lies deep in the carotid sheath, in the gutter between the internal jugular vein and the carotid arteries, throughout the neck.
It is posterior to both. (Last's p. 462)
The cervical sympathetic trunk lies behind it on the prevertebral fascia

The cervical sympathetic trunk lies behind the sheath on the prevertebral fascia, not in the sheath.
Carotid surgery does not usually damage it. (Last's p. 462)
The glossopharyngeal nerve curves backwards superficial to the IJV

The accessory nerve curves backward superficial to the internal jugular vein. IX curves forward between the internal and external carotid arteries.
XI then enters sternocleidomastoid. (Last's p. 462)
The parotid lies medial to the sheath

The pharynx lies medial to the carotid sheath; the parotid lies lateral.
The sheath lies in the parapharyngeal space behind the parotid. (Last's p. 462)
Its medial boundary is the lateral pterygoid plate

The lateral surface of the lateral pterygoid plate forms the medial wall of the infratemporal fossa.
Both pterygoid muscles arise from it. (Last's p. 457)
Its lateral boundary is the ramus of the mandible

The ramus and coronoid process of the mandible form the lateral wall of the infratemporal fossa.
That is why the fossa is hidden in the intact skull. (Last's p. 457)
Its posterior boundary is the posterior surface of the maxilla

The posterior surface of the maxilla forms the anterior boundary. The posterior boundary is formed by the carotid sheath and styloid apparatus.
The pterygomaxillary fissure lies between the maxilla and the lateral plate. (Last's p. 457)
Its roof is formed by the lesser wing of the sphenoid

The roof is formed by the infratemporal surfaces of the greater wing of the sphenoid and the squamous temporal bone.
Foramen ovale and spinosum open in this roof. (Last's p. 457)
Lateral pterygoid inserts into the pterygoid fovea

Both heads of lateral pterygoid insert into the pterygoid fovea on the neck of the mandible and into the articular disc.
So it pulls the condyle and disc forward together. (Last's p. 458)
The superficial head of medial pterygoid arises from the maxillary tuberosity

The superficial head of medial pterygoid arises from the maxillary tuberosity and the pyramidal process of the palatine bone.
The deep head arises from the medial surface of the lateral plate. (Last's p. 458)
Lateral pterygoid closes the mouth

Lateral pterygoid opens the mouth, drawing the condyle and disc forward onto the articular tubercle.
Masseter, temporalis and medial pterygoid close it. (Last's p. 458)
Medial pterygoid is supplied by the anterior division of the mandibular nerve

Medial pterygoid is supplied from the main trunk of V3, not the anterior division.
The same branch supplies the two tensors. (Last's p. 458)
It passes between the neck of the mandible and sphenomandibular ligament

The maxillary artery enters the infratemporal fossa between the neck of the mandible and the sphenomandibular ligament.
Its first part lies here. (Last's p. 459)
Branches of its first and third parts enter bony foramina

Branches of the first and third parts of the maxillary artery enter bony foramina; the second-part branches (to muscles) do not.
A useful organising rule. (Last's p. 459)
The anterior tympanic artery enters through the squamotympanic fissure

The anterior tympanic artery enters the middle ear through the petrotympanic fissure. The deep auricular artery enters the squamotympanic fissure region.
The chorda tympani shares the petrotympanic fissure. (Last's p. 459)
It usually passes above both heads of lateral pterygoid

The maxillary artery usually passes between the heads of lateral pterygoid or deep to the lower head; it rarely passes above both heads.
It is superficial to the lower head in many people. (Last's p. 459)

questions.s: Branches of the third part of the maxillary artery (Last's):
o: The pharyngeal artery enters the palatovaginal canal

The pharyngeal branch of the third part runs back through the palatovaginal canal with the pharyngeal nerve.
It supplies the nasopharynx. (Last's p. 459)
The infraorbital artery passes through the inferior orbital fissure

The infraorbital artery enters the orbit through the inferior orbital fissure and runs forward with the infraorbital nerve.
It emerges on the face at the infraorbital foramen. (Last's p. 459)
It terminates as the greater palatine artery

The maxillary artery terminates as the sphenopalatine artery, which enters the nose through the sphenopalatine foramen.
It is the main artery of epistaxis. (Last's p. 459)
The posterior superior alveolar artery arises from the second part

The posterior superior alveolar artery arises from the third part, as the maxillary artery enters the pterygopalatine fossa.
Second-part branches supply the muscles of mastication. (Last's p. 459)
It lies around and within lateral pterygoid

The pterygoid venous plexus surrounds and lies within lateral pterygoid.
It is a large plexus in the infratemporal fossa. (Last's p. 460)
It acts as a peripheral heart for venous return

Contraction of the pterygoid muscles pumps blood through the plexus, so it acts as a "peripheral heart".
Chewing helps venous return from the region. (Last's p. 460)
It drains into the facial vein directly

The plexus drains into the maxillary veins, which join the superficial temporal vein to form the retromandibular vein.
It connects with the facial vein only indirectly, through the deep facial vein. (Last's p. 460)
It has no connection with the inferior ophthalmic vein

The pterygoid plexus receives the inferior ophthalmic vein through the inferior orbital fissure.
It also connects with the cavernous sinus via emissary veins. (Last's p. 460)
It develops from the perichondrium of Meckel's cartilage

The sphenomandibular ligament is the perichondrium of Meckel's (first arch) cartilage.
The cartilage itself forms the malleus and incus. (Last's p. 460)
It is pierced by the mylohyoid nerve

The nerve to mylohyoid pierces the sphenomandibular ligament to reach the mylohyoid groove.
It then supplies mylohyoid and the anterior belly of digastric. (Last's p. 460)
The inferior alveolar nerve passes between it and the neck of the mandible

The auriculotemporal nerve and maxillary vessels pass between the ligament and the neck of the mandible. The inferior alveolar nerve passes between the ligament and the ramus.
The neck is higher, the ramus lower. (Last's p. 460)
The mylohyoid groove is made by the mylohyoid nerve

The mylohyoid groove is made by the mylohyoid vessels (the vein), not the nerve.
A Last's detail. (Last's p. 460)

questions.s: The mandibular nerve in the infratemporal fossa (Last's):
o: It lies about 4 cm deep to the articular tubercle

The mandibular nerve lies about 4 cm deep to the articular tubercle; it is reached through the mandibular notch in a mandibular nerve block.
The needle is aimed behind the lateral pterygoid plate. (Last's p. 460-2)
The otic ganglion lies on its deep surface

The small otic ganglion lies on the medial (deep) surface of the mandibular nerve, just below foramen ovale.
Tensor palati lies medial to it. (Last's p. 460-2)
The auriculotemporal nerve lies below the maxillary artery

The auriculotemporal nerve lies above the maxillary artery as both pass behind the neck of the mandible.
The maxillary vein is below. (Last's p. 460-2)
The lingual nerve enters the pharynx between middle and inferior constrictors

The lingual nerve enters the mouth by passing below the lower border of the superior constrictor, between the superior and middle constrictors.
The internal laryngeal nerve passes between the middle and inferior constrictors. (Last's p. 460-2)
It lies between tensor palati and the mandibular nerve

The otic ganglion is sandwiched between tensor palati medially and the mandibular nerve laterally.
It is small and hard to see. (Last's p. 460-2)
It lies just below foramen ovale

The otic ganglion lies just below foramen ovale.
The lesser petrosal nerve reaches it there. (Last's p. 460-2)
It is round and about 1 cm across

The otic ganglion is only 2 to 3 mm across, flat and applied to the nerve; it is not round and 1 cm across.
A size trap. (Last's p. 460-2)
Its parasympathetic root is the greater petrosal nerve

The parasympathetic root of the otic ganglion is the lesser petrosal nerve (IX). The greater petrosal goes to the pterygopalatine ganglion.
Lesser = parotid. (Last's p. 460-2)

questions.s: The glossopharyngeal nerve in the neck (Last's):
o: It curves forwards around the lateral side of stylopharyngeus

IX winds round the posterior then lateral side of stylopharyngeus, supplying it.
It then passes forward with the muscle between the carotids. (Last's p. 462-5)
Its pharyngeal branches join the plexus on the middle constrictor

The pharyngeal branches of IX join the plexus on the middle constrictor and are sensory.
They form the afferent limb of the gag reflex. (Last's p. 462-5)
The tympanic branch leaves at the superior ganglion

The tympanic branch of IX leaves at the inferior ganglion, not the superior.
It then enters the tympanic canaliculus. (Last's p. 462-5)
It reaches the tongue in front of hyoglossus

IX reaches the tongue by passing deep to the posterior border of hyoglossus, not in front of it.
It supplies the posterior third. (Last's p. 462-5)
The external laryngeal nerve runs close to the superior thyroid vessels

The external laryngeal nerve runs close to the superior thyroid vessels, so it is at risk when they are ligated in thyroidectomy.
The artery is tied close to the gland to avoid it. (Last's p. 462-5)
The auricular branch supplies part of the outer tympanic membrane

The auricular branch of X (Arnold's nerve) supplies part of the external meatus and the outer surface of the tympanic membrane.
Hence coughing when the ear is cleaned. (Last's p. 462-5)
The pharyngeal branch supplies stylopharyngeus

The pharyngeal branch of X supplies all pharyngeal muscles except stylopharyngeus, which is supplied by IX.
Stylopharyngeus is the classic exception. (Last's p. 462-5)
The right cervical cardiac branches pass in front of the subclavian artery

The right cervical cardiac branches of the vagus pass behind the subclavian artery, not in front.
They descend to the cardiac plexus. (Last's p. 462-5)
It derives from the second arch

The styloid process and stylohyoid ligament come from the second-arch cartilage (Reichert's).
So do the lesser horn and upper body of the hyoid. (Last's p. 462-5)
The external carotid passes superficial to stylopharyngeus

The external carotid passes superficial to stylopharyngeus, but deep to digastric and stylohyoid.
Stylopharyngeus separates it from the internal carotid. (Last's p. 462-5)
Stylopharyngeus arises low down in front

Stylopharyngeus arises from the deepest and highest part of the styloid process. Styloglossus arises low down in front.
Stylohyoid arises from the back. (Last's p. 462-5)
The three styloid muscles share one nerve supply

Each of the three styloid muscles has a different nerve supply: stylopharyngeus (IX), stylohyoid (VII), styloglossus (XII).
A favourite question. (Last's p. 462-5)

questions.s: The hypoglossal nerve in the neck (Last's):
o: It picks up a branch from C1

C1 fibres join XII and leave again in its "branches": the superior root of the ansa, the nerves to thyrohyoid and geniohyoid, and the meningeal branch.
XII itself supplies only tongue muscles. (Last's p. 462-5)
It passes forwards just above the greater horn of the hyoid

XII runs forward just above the greater horn of the hyoid, on hyoglossus.
It lies below the submandibular duct. (Last's p. 462-5)
It lies superficial to the IJV

XII lies deep to the veins, including the internal jugular and facial veins, as it crosses the arteries.
It lies superficial to the arteries. (Last's p. 462-5)
Its meningeal branch enters through the jugular foramen

The meningeal branch of XII (C1 fibres) re-enters the skull through the hypoglossal canal, not the jugular foramen.
It supplies dura around the foramen magnum. (Last's p. 462-5)
The hard palate lies at C1

The hard palate is level with the anterior arch of the atlas (C1).
Useful on lateral radiographs. (Last's p. 462-5)
The hyoid lies at C3

The hyoid lies at C3, the thyroid cartilage at C4 to C5 and the cricoid at C6.
These levels help locate structures. (Last's p. 462-5)
The cricoid lies at C4

The cricoid cartilage lies at C6, not C4.
C6 also marks the start of the trachea and oesophagus. (Last's p. 462-5)
The carotid pulse is felt against the C3 transverse process

The carotid pulse is felt against the transverse process (carotid tubercle) of C6, not C3.
Pressure here can compress the common carotid. (Last's p. 462-5)

questions.s: The investing layer of deep cervical fascia (Last's):
o: It splits to enclose sternocleidomastoid and trapezius

The investing layer splits to enclose sternocleidomastoid and trapezius, and the parotid and submandibular glands.
It is the outermost layer of deep cervical fascia. (Last's p. 462-5)
It attaches to the hyoid

The investing layer is attached to the hyoid, which pulls sternocleidomastoid forward into a gentle curve.
It divides the front of the neck into upper and lower compartments. (Last's p. 462-5)
It forms the axillary sheath

The axillary sheath is formed by the prevertebral fascia, carried over the subclavian artery and brachial plexus.
The investing layer has no such extension. (Last's p. 462-5)
It attaches above to the inferior nuchal line

The investing layer attaches above to the superior nuchal line, not the inferior.
It also attaches to the mastoid, zygomatic arch and mandible. (Last's p. 462-5)
It extends down to T3

The prevertebral fascia extends down to T3, with longus colli.
Below, it fuses with the anterior longitudinal ligament. (Last's p. 462-5)
It is pierced by the four cutaneous branches of the cervical plexus

The great auricular, lesser occipital, transverse cervical and supraclavicular nerves all pierce the prevertebral fascia.
They are the cutaneous branches of the cervical plexus. (Last's p. 462-5)
The accessory nerve lies deep to it

Last's says the accessory nerve lies superficial to the prevertebral fascia.
That is why it is so easily injured in the posterior triangle. (Last's p. 462-5)
The cervical sympathetic trunk lies deep to it

Last's says the cervical sympathetic trunk lies superficial to (in front of) the prevertebral fascia.
It lies behind the carotid sheath. (Last's p. 462-5)
It is limited above by the strap muscle attachments

The pretracheal fascia is limited above by the attachments of the strap muscles (hyoid and thyroid cartilage).
It lies deep to the straps. (Last's p. 462-5)
It blends below with the fibrous pericardium

Below, the pretracheal fascia passes behind the brachiocephalic veins to blend with the adventitia of the aortic arch and the fibrous pericardium.
A route for infection into the mediastinum. (Last's p. 462-5)
The thyroid is attached to it at the first tracheal ring

The thyroid isthmus attaches to the pretracheal fascia at tracheal rings 2 to 4, not the first ring.
This is why the thyroid moves with swallowing. (Last's p. 462-5)
It lies superficial to the strap muscles

The pretracheal fascia lies beneath (deep to) the strap muscles, not superficial to them.
The investing layer is superficial. (Last's p. 462-5)
The retropharyngeal space continues into the posterior mediastinum

The retropharyngeal space, in front of the prevertebral fascia and behind the pharynx and oesophagus, runs from the skull base into the posterior mediastinum. It is a route for spread of infection.
Retropharyngeal abscess can therefore cause mediastinitis. (Last's p. 462-5)
The prevertebral space extends from skull base to T3

The prevertebral space lies behind the prevertebral fascia, from the skull base to T3.
Infection here (for example spinal tuberculosis) is limited below by the fascia's fusion. (Last's p. 462-5)
The retropharyngeal space lies behind the prevertebral fascia

The retropharyngeal space lies in front of the prevertebral fascia, behind the buccopharyngeal fascia.
Behind the prevertebral fascia is the prevertebral space. (Last's p. 462-5)
The parapharyngeal space is bounded medially by the pterygoid muscles

The parapharyngeal space is bounded laterally by the pterygoid muscles (and mandible and parotid); medially by the pharynx.
It is a lateral space. (Last's p. 462-5)
It receives ipsilateral cortical innervation

Last's says sternocleidomastoid receives ipsilateral cortical innervation, unlike any other muscle.
This fits its action of turning the head to the opposite side. (Last's p. 462-5)
It is supplied by the occipital and superior thyroid arteries

Sternocleidomastoid is supplied by branches of the occipital and superior thyroid arteries.
It has a segmental blood supply. (Last's p. 462-5)
The accessory nerve emerges at the junction of its lower and middle thirds

The accessory nerve emerges halfway down the posterior border of sternocleidomastoid, not at the junction of its lower and middle thirds.
Erb's point lies close by. (Last's p. 462-5)
It inserts into the lateral third of the clavicle

The clavicular head inserts into the medial third of the clavicle.
Trapezius attaches to the lateral third. (Last's p. 462-5)
The cervical plexus does not actually lie in the triangle

The cervical plexus does not actually lie in the posterior triangle; it is covered by sternocleidomastoid.
Only its cutaneous branches emerge into the triangle. (Last's p. 462-5)
The accessory nerve runs over levator scapulae in the roof fascia

Emerging from sternocleidomastoid halfway down its posterior border, XI crosses the triangle on levator scapulae within the roof fascia, very superficial and easily injured.
Injury causes shoulder droop and weakness of trapezius. (Last's p. 462-5)
Its roof is prevertebral fascia

The roof of the posterior triangle is the investing layer of deep fascia. The prevertebral fascia forms the floor.
So XI, in the roof, is superficial to the floor muscles. (Last's p. 462-5)
Its base is the medial third of the clavicle

The base of the posterior triangle is the middle third of the clavicle.
Sternocleidomastoid and trapezius take the medial and lateral thirds. (Last's p. 462-5)
The lesser occipital nerve is C2

The lesser occipital nerve (anterior ramus of C2) hooks around XI and runs up the back of sternocleidomastoid to the scalp behind the ear.
It is a landmark for finding XI. (Last's p. 462-5)
The supraclavicular nerves are C3, 4

The supraclavicular nerves are from C3 and C4, mainly C4.
They supply the skin over the clavicle and shoulder. (Last's p. 462-5)
The great auricular nerve is C4

The great auricular nerve is from C2 and C3.
C4 contributes to the supraclavicular and phrenic nerves. (Last's p. 462-5)
The lesser occipital nerve comes from a posterior ramus

The lesser occipital nerve comes from the anterior ramus of C2.
The greater occipital is the posterior ramus of C2. (Last's p. 462-5)
The great auricular nerve may thicken in tuberculoid leprosy

The great auricular nerve crosses sternocleidomastoid superficially and may become palpably thickened in tuberculoid leprosy.
It is a classic site to feel for nerve thickening. (Last's p. 462-5)
The lateral supraclavicular nerves reach halfway down deltoid

The lateral supraclavicular nerves cross the acromion to supply skin halfway down deltoid and back to the scapular spine.
This is C4 skin over the shoulder. (Last's p. 462-5)
The transverse cervical nerve closely accompanies the transverse cervical artery

Last's says the transverse cervical nerve is some distance from the transverse cervical artery; they do not run together.
Similar names, different courses. (Last's p. 462-5)
The third occipital nerve is an anterior ramus branch

The third occipital nerve is a branch of the posterior ramus of C3.
The cervical plexus nerves are all anterior rami. (Last's p. 462-5)
It is a branch of the nerve to subclavius

An accessory phrenic contribution (C5, C6) may run with the nerve to subclavius in front of the subclavian vein.
It is present in some people. (Last's p. 462-5)
It joins the phrenic in the superior mediastinum

The accessory phrenic nerve joins the main phrenic nerve in the superior mediastinum (or root of the neck).
So injury to the main phrenic in the neck may spare some diaphragm function. (Last's p. 462-5)
It arises from C3

The accessory phrenic arises from C5 and C6, not C3.
The main phrenic is C3 to C5. (Last's p. 462-5)
It passes behind the subclavian vein

The accessory phrenic passes in front of the subclavian vein.
The main phrenic passes behind the vein. (Last's p. 462-5)
Stylohyoid embraces the digastric tendon

Stylohyoid splits around the intermediate tendon of digastric before inserting into the hyoid.
It is a second-arch muscle supplied by VII. (Last's p. 462-5)
Geniohyoid is supplied by C1 via the hypoglossal

Geniohyoid is supplied by C1 fibres that travel with XII.
So is thyrohyoid. (Last's p. 462-5)
The anterior belly of digastric is supplied by the facial nerve

The anterior belly of digastric is supplied by the nerve to mylohyoid (V3); the posterior belly by VII.
The two bellies come from different arches. (Last's p. 462-5)
Mylohyoid's anterior fibres insert into the hyoid

Only the posterior quarter of mylohyoid inserts into the hyoid; the rest inserts into the midline raphe.
The anterior fibres meet in the raphe. (Last's p. 462-5)
Sternothyroid is broader than sternohyoid and deep to it

Sternothyroid is the broader muscle, lying deep to sternohyoid and end to end with thyrohyoid.
Its upper end attaches to the oblique line of the thyroid cartilage. (Last's p. 462-5)
Omohyoid becomes tendinous over the IJV

The intermediate tendon of omohyoid lies over the internal jugular vein, a useful guide to the vein, and is slung to the clavicle by fascia.
It is a landmark in neck dissection. (Last's p. 462-5)
Thyrohyoid is supplied by the ansa cervicalis

Thyrohyoid is supplied by C1 fibres via the hypoglossal nerve, not by the ansa cervicalis.
The ansa supplies the other three strap muscles. (Last's p. 462-5)
Sternothyroid inserts into the first costal cartilage only

Sternothyroid arises from the manubrium and the first costal cartilage.
So "first costal cartilage only" is wrong. (Last's p. 462-5)
The right arises behind the sternoclavicular joint

The right common carotid arises from the brachiocephalic trunk behind the right sternoclavicular joint. The left arises directly from the aortic arch.
So the left has a thoracic part. (Last's p. 462-5)
It gives no branches below its bifurcation

The common carotid gives no branches below its bifurcation into the internal and external carotids.
Occasionally the superior thyroid arises from it. (Last's p. 462-5)
The sympathetic trunk lies within the sheath

The sympathetic trunk lies behind the carotid sheath, outside it.
It is on the prevertebral fascia. (Last's p. 462-5)
The vagus lies medial to the common carotid

The vagus lies between the common carotid and the internal jugular vein, behind them.
It is not medial to the artery. (Last's p. 462-5)
Its inferior root spirals from behind the IJV

The inferior root of the ansa (C2, C3) spirals round the lateral side of the internal jugular vein from behind, to join the superior root in front of the vein.
The loop lies on the sheath. (Last's p. 462-5)
Its superior root runs down in front of the IJV

The superior root (C1 via XII) descends in front of the internal jugular vein and carotids, embedded in the sheath.
It leaves XII as the nerve crosses the internal carotid. (Last's p. 462-5)
It lies within the posterior wall of the carotid sheath

The ansa lies within the anterior wall of the carotid sheath, not the posterior wall.
It is visible as soon as the sheath is exposed. (Last's p. 462-5)
Its superior root is formed by C2

The superior root is formed by C1 fibres hitch-hiking with XII.
C2 and C3 form the inferior root. (Last's p. 462-5)
Sympathetic fibres from the superior cervical ganglion travel with the superior thyroid artery

Vasoconstrictor fibres from the superior cervical ganglion reach the thyroid along the superior thyroid artery.
They regulate blood flow, not secretion. (Last's p. 462-5)
Middle cervical ganglion fibres travel with the inferior thyroid artery

Fibres from the middle cervical ganglion travel along the inferior thyroid artery.
The middle ganglion lies close to that artery. (Last's p. 462-5)
Thyroid secretion is under vagal control

Last's says the role of the vagus in the thyroid is unknown; thyroid secretion is controlled hormonally (TSH). The sympathetic fibres are vasoconstrictor.
So there is no vagal control of secretion. (Last's p. 462-5)
Mylohyoid separates the neck from the nasopharynx

Mylohyoid separates the mouth from the neck, forming the floor of the mouth.
The soft palate separates the nasopharynx from the mouth. (Last's p. 462-5)
The superior thyroid artery is its first anterior branch

The superior thyroid artery is the first (lowest) anterior branch of the external carotid, arising near the bifurcation.
It runs down to the upper pole of the thyroid. (Last's p. 437-8)
The external laryngeal nerve lies behind the superior thyroid artery

The external laryngeal nerve runs just behind the superior thyroid artery, so it is at risk when the upper pole is ligated.
Ligate close to the gland. (Last's p. 437-8)
The lingual artery runs superficial to hyoglossus

The lingual artery runs deep to hyoglossus. XII lies superficial to the muscle.
So the muscle separates artery from nerve. (Last's p. 437-8)
The facial artery gives the submental artery after crossing the mandible

The facial artery gives the submental artery just before crossing the mandible, not after.
The submental artery runs forward under the mandible. (Last's p. 437-8)

questions.s: The occipital and posterior auricular arteries (Last's):
o: The posterior auricular gives the stylomastoid branch

The posterior auricular artery gives the stylomastoid branch, which supplies the facial nerve in its canal and the stapedial region.
It enters the stylomastoid foramen. (Last's p. 437-8)
The occipital artery runs with the greater occipital nerve

The occipital artery reaches the scalp with the greater occipital nerve, lateral to semispinalis capitis.
They pierce trapezius together. (Last's p. 437-8)
The posterior auricular arises below digastric

The posterior auricular artery arises above digastric, sometimes within the parotid, not below it.
The occipital artery runs along the lower border. (Last's p. 437-8)
The lower SCM branch of the occipital artery guides to the accessory nerve

Last's says the upper sternocleidomastoid branch of the occipital artery guides to the accessory nerve. The lower branch holds XII down.
The two branches mark different nerves. (Last's p. 437-8)

questions.s: Relations of the internal jugular vein (Last's):
o: The jugulo-omohyoid node lies behind it above omohyoid

The jugulo-omohyoid node lies behind the internal jugular vein just above omohyoid; it drains the tongue.
It is the classic node involved in tongue cancer. (Last's p. 438)
The phrenic nerve lies behind it on scalenus anterior

The phrenic nerve on scalenus anterior and the cervical plexus lie behind the internal jugular vein.
They are separated from it by the prevertebral fascia. (Last's p. 438)
The transverse cervical artery lies in front of the IJV

The transverse cervical artery lies between scalenus anterior and the internal jugular vein, behind the vein.
It crosses in front of the phrenic nerve. (Last's p. 438)
The facial vein is its first tributary

The first tributary of the internal jugular vein is the inferior petrosal sinus, not the facial vein.
The facial vein joins near the hyoid. (Last's p. 438)
The carotid triangle is bounded by SCM, posterior belly of digastric and superior belly of omohyoid

The carotid triangle is bounded by sternocleidomastoid, the posterior belly of digastric and the superior belly of omohyoid. It contains the carotid bifurcation.
Most carotid surgery is done here. (Last's p. 438)
The submental triangle contains the anterior jugular vein

The submental triangle, between the anterior bellies of digastric and the hyoid, contains the anterior jugular vein and the submental lymph nodes.
Its floor is mylohyoid. (Last's p. 438)
The posterior auricular artery arises within the carotid triangle

All branches of the external carotid except the posterior auricular arise within the carotid triangle. The posterior auricular arises higher, above digastric.
So the statement is reversed. (Last's p. 438)
The digastric triangle is bounded below by the hyoid body

The digastric (submandibular) triangle is bounded by the two bellies of digastric and the mandible. The hyoid body bounds the submental triangle.
The submandibular gland fills the digastric triangle. (Last's p. 438)
Rectus capitis lateralis runs from atlas to the jugular process

Rectus capitis lateralis runs from the transverse process of the atlas to the jugular process of the occipital bone.
It lies just behind the jugular foramen. (Last's p. 440)
Longus capitis arises from C3-6 anterior tubercles

Longus capitis arises from the anterior tubercles of C3 to C6 and inserts into the basiocciput.
It flexes the head. (Last's p. 440)
Rectus capitis anterior runs from the axis to the foramen magnum

Rectus capitis anterior runs from the lateral mass of the atlas to the basiocciput (in front of the condyle), not from the axis.
It is a short muscle. (Last's p. 440)
Longus colli is supplied by posterior rami

Longus colli is supplied by anterior rami of the cervical nerves.
All the prevertebral muscles are supplied by anterior rami. (Last's p. 440)

questions.s: The pyramidal space beside scalenus anterior (Last's):
o: Its apex is the carotid tubercle

The pyramidal space between longus colli and scalenus anterior has its apex at the carotid tubercle of C6.
This is the landmark for stellate ganglion block. (Last's p. 440)
It contains the vertebral artery and stellate ganglion

The pyramidal space contains the vertebral artery and vein and the stellate (inferior cervical) ganglion.
The vertebral artery runs up to enter the C6 transverse foramen. (Last's p. 440)
It has a fascial roof

Last's says there is no fascial roof over the pyramidal space.
So structures in it lie directly under the carotid sheath. (Last's p. 440)
Its base is the clavicle

The base of the space is the subclavian artery and the neck of the first rib, with the suprapleural membrane between them, not the clavicle.
The pleural dome lies just below. (Last's p. 440)
The superior ganglion gives grey rami to C1-4

The superior cervical ganglion gives grey rami to C1 to C4, the middle to C5 and C6, and the inferior to C7 and C8.
There are no white rami in the neck. (Last's p. 440)
The middle ganglion lies near the C6 carotid tubercle

The small, inconstant middle cervical ganglion lies medial to the carotid tubercle of C6.
It is close to the inferior thyroid artery. (Last's p. 440)
The inferior ganglion gives grey rami to C5-6

The inferior ganglion gives grey rami to C7 and C8. The middle ganglion supplies C5 and C6.
Each ganglion supplies the nerves nearest it. (Last's p. 440)
The ansa subclavia passes behind the subclavian artery

The ansa subclavia passes in front of the subclavian artery, looping around it to join the middle and inferior ganglia.
It is not behind the artery. (Last's p. 440)
The left superior ganglion's cardiac branch goes to the superficial cardiac plexus

Of the cervical sympathetic cardiac branches, only the left superior goes to the superficial cardiac plexus; the rest go to the deep plexus.
The superficial plexus lies below the aortic arch. (Last's p. 440)
The inferior ganglion gives a vertebral plexus

The inferior (stellate) ganglion sends a large branch along the vertebral artery, the vertebral plexus.
This supplies the vertebrobasilar vessels. (Last's p. 440)
Middle ganglion branches on the inferior thyroid artery are somatic

Branches of the middle ganglion running on the inferior thyroid artery are visceral (to the thyroid and parathyroids), not somatic.
Somatic distribution is by grey rami to spinal nerves. (Last's p. 440)
The sympathetic trunk lies in front of the carotid sheath

The sympathetic trunk lies behind the carotid sheath, not in front of it.
It lies on the prevertebral muscles. (Last's p. 440)
It is supplied by C4, 5, 6

Scalenus anterior is supplied by the anterior rami of C4, C5 and C6.
It is a landmark at the root of the neck. (Last's p. 444)
The subclavian vein lies in front of it

The subclavian vein lies in front of scalenus anterior, free to dilate.
The vein is outside the prevertebral fascia. (Last's p. 444)
The subclavian artery passes in front of it

The second part of the subclavian artery passes behind scalenus anterior, not in front.
The vein is in front. (Last's p. 444)
The third part of the subclavian artery lies in front of the prevertebral fascia

The third part of the subclavian artery lies behind the prevertebral fascia, with the brachial plexus trunks.
That is why it enters the axillary sheath. (Last's p. 444)
Scalenus medius arises from all cervical vertebrae

Scalenus medius arises from the posterior tubercles and lamellae of all the cervical vertebrae.
It is the largest scalene. (Last's p. 444)
Scalenus posterior inserts into the second rib

Scalenus posterior crosses the first rib to insert into the outer border of the second rib.
It is the smallest and most posterior. (Last's p. 444)
Scalenus posterior inserts into the first rib

Scalenus posterior inserts into the second rib, not the first.
Scalenus anterior and medius insert into the first rib. (Last's p. 444)
The dorsal scapular artery passes in front of scalenus anterior

The dorsal scapular artery passes in front of scalenus medius, through the brachial plexus, not in front of scalenus anterior.
It supplies the rhomboids and levator scapulae. (Last's p. 444)
The suprapleural membrane forms its floor

The suprapleural membrane (Sibson's fascia) closes the thoracic inlet over the dome of the pleura, forming the floor of the root of the neck.
It attaches to the inner border of the first rib. (Last's p. 444)
The recurrent laryngeal nerves run between trachea and oesophagus

In the root of the neck the recurrent laryngeal nerves run up in the groove between the trachea and oesophagus.
They are at risk in thyroid surgery. (Last's p. 444)
The costocervical trunk arises from the first part of the subclavian

The costocervical trunk arises from the second part of the subclavian artery, behind scalenus anterior.
The vertebral, internal thoracic and thyrocervical arise from the first part. (Last's p. 444)
The internal thoracic artery arises from the upper surface of the subclavian

The internal thoracic artery arises from the lower surface of the subclavian artery.
It descends behind the costal cartilages. (Last's p. 444)
They develop from second arch mesoderm

The muscles of facial expression develop from second-arch mesoderm and so are supplied by VII.
They migrate widely over the face and scalp. (Last's p. 445-9)
The pterygomandibular raphe interdigitates with the superior constrictor

The pterygomandibular raphe joins buccinator in front to the superior constrictor behind; the two muscles interdigitate at the raphe.
It runs from the hamulus to the mandible. (Last's p. 445-9)
The marginal mandibular branch lies below the angle in about 50%

The marginal mandibular branch lies below the angle of the mandible in about 20 percent of people, not 50 percent.
Still a reason to place incisions low. (Last's p. 445-9)
Buccal branch paralysis prevents blinking

Paralysis of the buccal branches prevents emptying of the cheek pouch. Loss of the zygomatic branches (orbicularis oculi) prevents blinking.
Different branches, different functions. (Last's p. 445-9)
Skin over the angle of the mandible is supplied by the great auricular nerve

The great auricular nerve (C2, C3) supplies the skin over the angle of the mandible, the only facial skin not supplied by V.
A V3 lesion therefore spares the angle. (Last's p. 450-1)
The lower eyelid is supplied by V2

The lower eyelid is supplied by the palpebral branches of the infraorbital nerve (V2).
The upper lid is V1. (Last's p. 450-1)
The ophthalmic division has three cutaneous branches

The ophthalmic division has five cutaneous branches (supraorbital, supratrochlear, lacrimal, infratrochlear, external nasal); the maxillary and mandibular have three each.
Five plus three plus three. (Last's p. 450-1)
The infratrochlear nerve supplies the lower eyelid

The infratrochlear nerve supplies the medial part of the upper eyelid and the bridge of the nose, not the lower lid.
The lower lid is V2. (Last's p. 450-1)
The angular vein becomes the facial vein below the mandible

The supraorbital and supratrochlear veins form the angular vein at the medial canthus, which continues as the facial vein.
It runs down behind the facial artery. (Last's p. 450-1)
The posterior branch of the retromandibular vein joins the posterior auricular to form the EJV

The posterior division of the retromandibular vein joins the posterior auricular vein to form the external jugular vein.
The anterior division joins the facial vein. (Last's p. 450-1)
The superficial temporal vein joins the facial vein to form the retromandibular vein

The superficial temporal vein joins the maxillary vein to form the retromandibular vein, not the facial vein.
This union happens in the parotid. (Last's p. 450-1)
The deep facial vein connects the facial vein to the cavernous sinus directly

The deep facial vein connects the facial vein to the pterygoid plexus, which then connects with the cavernous sinus through emissary veins.
The connection is indirect. (Last's p. 450-1)
Its neurovascular plane is the dense connective tissue layer

The vessels and nerves of the scalp run in the dense connective tissue (second layer), where vessels are held open, so scalp wounds bleed freely.
The layers: skin, connective tissue, aponeurosis, loose areolar tissue, pericranium. (Last's p. 452-4)
Scalp skin is the thickest in the body

Scalp skin is the thickest skin in the body.
It is rich in hair follicles and sebaceous glands. (Last's p. 452-4)
The two occipitalis muscles join in the midline

The frontal bellies of occipitofrontalis meet in the midline; the occipital bellies do not.
The galea fills the gap between the occipital bellies. (Last's p. 452-4)
Frontalis has a bony origin

Only occipitalis has a bony origin (the highest nuchal line). Frontalis arises from the skin and orbicularis oculi.
Frontalis has no bony attachment. (Last's p. 452-4)

questions.s: Nerves and vessels of the scalp (Last's):
o: The middle temporal vessels pierce temporalis fascia

The middle temporal vessels pierce the temporalis fascia to reach the muscle.
The superficial temporal vessels lie on the fascia. (Last's p. 452-4)
Frontalis is supplied by temporal and zygomatic branches of VII

Frontalis is supplied by the temporal and upper zygomatic branches of VII; occipitalis by the posterior auricular branch.
Frontal branch injury causes a drooping brow. (Last's p. 452-4)
The greater occipital nerve is an anterior ramus

The greater occipital nerve is the posterior ramus of C2, not an anterior ramus.
The lesser occipital is the anterior ramus. (Last's p. 452-4)
The superficial temporal vessels pierce temporalis fascia

The superficial temporal vessels lie on the temporalis fascia; they do not pierce it.
The middle temporal vessels pierce it. (Last's p. 452-4)
Its posterior fibres retract the mandible

The posterior fibres of temporalis retract the mandible; they are the only retractor.
Lateral pterygoid does the opposite. (Last's p. 454-5)
It is supplied by deep temporal nerves

Temporalis is supplied by two or three deep temporal branches of the anterior division of V3.
They enter its deep surface. (Last's p. 454-5)
Its anterior fibres are horizontal

The anterior fibres of temporalis are vertical; the posterior fibres are horizontal.
The posterior fibres run forward above the ear. (Last's p. 454-5)
It inserts into the condylar process

Temporalis inserts into the coronoid process and the front of the ramus of the mandible, not the condylar process.
Lateral pterygoid inserts into the condyle. (Last's p. 454-5)
It has three heads fused anteriorly

Last's describes three heads of masseter (superficial, intermediate and deep), fused anteriorly and diverging behind.
The deep head is from the deep surface of the arch. (Last's p. 454-5)
The masseteric nerve runs between deep and intermediate parts

The masseteric nerve runs between the deep and intermediate parts; the masseteric artery between the intermediate and superficial parts.
A Last's detail. (Last's p. 454-5)
It retracts the mandible

Masseter elevates and protracts the mandible; it does not retract it.
Only posterior temporalis retracts. (Last's p. 454-5)
Its superficial part arises from the posterior third of the arch

The superficial part of masseter arises from the anterior two-thirds of the lower border of the zygomatic arch (and maxillary process), not the posterior third.
The deep part arises from the posterior part and deep surface. (Last's p. 454-5)
From superficial to deep: facial nerve, retromandibular vein, ECA

From superficial to deep in the parotid: facial nerve, retromandibular vein, external carotid artery.
The nerve is the most superficial and the most at risk. (Last's p. 455-7)
Its upper pole adheres to the cartilage of the external meatus

The small upper pole of the parotid is moulded against the cartilaginous external meatus near the capsule of the temporomandibular joint.
The auriculotemporal nerve emerges here. (Last's p. 455-7)
The ECA is its most superficial content

The facial nerve is the most superficial content of the parotid. The external carotid is the deepest.
Remember the order: nerve, vein, artery. (Last's p. 455-7)
The parotid fascia is supplied by the auriculotemporal nerve

The parotid fascia is supplied by the great auricular nerve; the gland itself by the auriculotemporal nerve.
Mumps pain arises from the tense fascia. (Last's p. 455-7)
Secretomotor fibres relay in the otic ganglion

Parotid secretomotor fibres start in the inferior salivary nucleus, travel in IX, its tympanic branch and the lesser petrosal nerve, relay in the otic ganglion, and reach the gland via the auriculotemporal nerve.
The facial nerve passes through the gland but does not supply it. (Last's p. 455-7)
Sympathetic fibres travel with the middle meningeal artery

Sympathetic fibres from the superior cervical ganglion reach the parotid via the plexus on the external carotid and the middle meningeal artery.
They pass through the otic ganglion without synapse. (Last's p. 455-7)
Secretomotor fibres arise in the superior salivary nucleus

Parotid secretomotor fibres arise in the inferior salivary nucleus. The superior salivary nucleus supplies the submandibular, sublingual and lacrimal glands.
Inferior = IX = parotid. (Last's p. 455-7)
Postganglionic fibres travel in the facial nerve

Postganglionic secretomotor fibres travel in the auriculotemporal nerve, not the facial nerve.
This explains Frey's syndrome after parotidectomy: regenerating auriculotemporal fibres reach sweat glands. (Last's p. 455-7)
The ganglion lies in front of the pterygoid canal

The pterygopalatine ganglion lies in front of the opening of the pterygoid canal, below and medial to the maxillary nerve.
It hangs from V2 by its ganglionic branches. (Last's p. 466-70)
It is called the ganglion of hay fever

Last's calls it the ganglion of hay fever because it is secretomotor to the nasal glands (and lacrimal gland).
Its overactivity causes rhinorrhoea and watering eyes. (Last's p. 466-70)
The lesser palatine nerves supply the hard palate

The lesser palatine nerves supply the soft palate and tonsil; the greater palatine supplies the hard palate.
Lesser = soft, greater = hard. (Last's p. 466-70)
The olfactory area extends below the superior concha

The olfactory area extends over the superior concha but not below it.
It covers the roof and upper septum. (Last's p. 466-70)
The zygomatic nerve runs above the maxillary nerve in the fissure

The zygomatic nerve runs above the maxillary nerve in the inferior orbital fissure before turning up the lateral orbital wall.
It carries lacrimal secretomotor fibres. (Last's p. 466-70)
The middle meningeal nerve supplies the front half of the middle fossa

The middle meningeal branch of V2 supplies the dura of the anterior half of the middle cranial fossa.
The nervus spinosus (V3) supplies the posterior half. (Last's p. 466-70)
The posterior superior alveolar nerve passes through the inferior orbital fissure

The posterior superior alveolar nerve leaves the pterygopalatine fossa through the pterygomaxillary fissure, not the inferior orbital fissure.
It then runs on the back of the maxilla. (Last's p. 466-70)
The ganglionic branches are multiple slender twigs

Last's says the ganglionic branches of V2, though named in the plural, form a single stout trunk to the pterygopalatine ganglion.
A small but testable detail. (Last's p. 466-70)
The sphenoidal sinus opens into the sphenoethmoidal recess

The sphenoidal sinus opens into the sphenoethmoidal recess above the superior concha.
This is the highest drainage site. (Last's p. 470-3)
The nasolacrimal duct opens into the inferior meatus

The nasolacrimal duct opens into the inferior meatus, guarded by a mucosal fold (the valve of Hasner).
It is the only structure opening into the inferior meatus. (Last's p. 470-3)
Posterior ethmoidal cells open into the middle meatus

Posterior ethmoidal cells open into the superior meatus.
Anterior and middle cells open into the middle meatus. (Last's p. 470-3)
The sphenopalatine foramen lies beneath the posterior end of the inferior concha

The sphenopalatine foramen lies beneath the posterior end of the middle concha, not the inferior concha.
It is the source of posterior epistaxis. (Last's p. 470-3)

questions.s: Nerve supply of the nasal cavity (Last's):
o: The vestibule is supplied by the infraorbital nerve

Branches of the infraorbital nerve creep in from the face to supply the vestibule of the nose.
The vestibule is skin-lined. (Last's p. 470-3)
The anterior superior alveolar nerve supplies the lower front of the lateral wall

The anterior superior alveolar nerve supplies the front of the lateral wall and floor of the nose (the lower front).
A small nasal branch. (Last's p. 470-3)
The nasopalatine nerve supplies the lateral wall

The nasopalatine nerve supplies the nasal septum (its posteroinferior part), not the lateral wall.
It runs down the septum to the incisive canal. (Last's p. 470-3)
The olfactory area extends onto the inferior concha

The olfactory area covers the roof, the upper septum and the superior concha only; it does not extend onto the inferior concha.
Olfactory epithelium is limited to the upper nose. (Last's p. 470-3)
Its floor lies lower than the floor of the nose

The alveolar floor of the maxillary sinus usually lies lower than the floor of the nose, near the roots of the molar teeth.
Molar extraction can open an oroantral fistula. (Last's p. 474-6)
Its ostium opens at the posterior end of the semilunar hiatus

The maxillary ostium opens high on the medial wall at the back of the semilunar hiatus, so the sinus drains poorly when upright.
Gravity drainage requires lying on the opposite side. (Last's p. 474-6)
Its apex points to the frontal process of the maxilla

The apex of the maxillary sinus points to the zygomatic process of the maxilla, not the frontal process.
It is a pyramid with the base medially. (Last's p. 474-6)
Its ostium lies low on the medial wall

The maxillary ostium lies high on the medial wall, so drainage is poor.
Antral washouts are done through the inferior meatus. (Last's p. 474-6)

questions.s: The ethmoidal, sphenoidal and frontal sinuses (Last's):
o: Posterior ethmoidal cells receive both V1 and V2 fibres

The posterior ethmoidal cells receive both V1 (posterior ethmoidal nerve) and V2 (orbital branches of the pterygopalatine ganglion) fibres.
Hence referred pain to both territories. (Last's p. 474-6)
The frontal sinus is supplied by the supraorbital nerve

The frontal sinus is supplied by the supraorbital and supratrochlear nerves.
Frontal sinusitis causes pain over the forehead. (Last's p. 474-6)
The sphenoidal sinuses are usually symmetrical

Last's says the sphenoidal sinuses are usually asymmetrical, with a deviated septum between them.
Surgeons should not rely on the septum as a midline marker. (Last's p. 474-6)
The frontal sinus drains into the posterior end of the semilunar hiatus

The frontal sinus drains into the front end of the semilunar hiatus, through the frontonasal duct or infundibulum.
The maxillary sinus drains at the back end. (Last's p. 474-6)
The pituitary fossa lies above it

The pituitary fossa sits on the roof of the sphenoidal sinus, allowing the trans-sphenoidal approach.
The degree of pneumatisation matters. (Last's p. 474-6)
The internal carotid artery lies lateral to it

The cavernous sinus and internal carotid artery lie lateral to the sphenoidal sinus and may ridge its wall.
They are at risk in sphenoid surgery. (Last's p. 474-6)
The pons lies above it

The pons lies behind the sphenoidal sinus, in the posterior cranial fossa, not above it.
The pituitary is above. (Last's p. 474-6)
The nerve of the pterygoid canal may ridge its roof

The nerve of the pterygoid canal may ridge the floor of the sphenoidal sinus, not its roof.
The optic nerve may ridge the lateral wall above. (Last's p. 474-6)

questions.s: Nerve supply of the mouth, teeth and gums (Last's):
o: The greater palatine nerve supplies palate to the incisive foramen

The greater palatine nerve supplies the hard palate and palatal gum forward to the incisive foramen. The nasopalatine supplies in front of it.
Palatal anaesthesia needs both nerves. (Last's p. 477)
The lingual nerve supplies the lower lingual gums

The lingual nerve supplies the lingual gum of the lower teeth.
It also supplies the floor of the mouth. (Last's p. 477)
The middle superior alveolar nerve supplies the canines

The upper canine is supplied by the anterior superior alveolar nerve. The middle superior alveolar nerve supplies the premolars.
Front teeth are anterior. (Last's p. 477)
The buccal nerve supplies the red margin of the lower lip

The red margin of the lower lip is supplied by the mental nerve. The buccal nerve supplies the cheek and molar gum.
Mental = chin and lower lip. (Last's p. 477)
The foramen caecum is the remnant of the thyroglossal duct

The foramen caecum at the apex of the sulcus terminalis marks where the thyroglossal duct began.
Lingual thyroid may lie there. (Last's p. 480-4)
The vallecula's anterior wall is supplied by the internal laryngeal nerve

The anterior wall of the vallecula is supplied by the internal laryngeal nerve (fourth arch).
So that small area of the tongue base is vagal. (Last's p. 480-4)
Palatoglossus is supplied by the hypoglossal nerve

Palatoglossus is supplied by the pharyngeal plexus (vagus), not the hypoglossal nerve.
It is the exception among tongue muscles. (Last's p. 480-4)
The second arch contributes to the tongue mucosa

Last's says the second arch is not represented in the tongue mucosa; it is overgrown by the third.
The chorda tympani gets there by joining a first-arch nerve. (Last's p. 480-4)
The lingual nerve lies on its superficial surface

On the superficial surface of hyoglossus lie the lingual nerve, the submandibular duct and XII.
From above down in that order. (Last's p. 480-4)
The lingual artery lies deep to it

The lingual artery lies deep to hyoglossus, with IX and the stylohyoid ligament.
To ligate it, you split the muscle. (Last's p. 480-4)
The hypoglossal nerve lies deep to it

XII lies on the superficial surface of hyoglossus, not deep to it.
The artery is deep. (Last's p. 480-4)
It arises from the lesser horn of the hyoid

Hyoglossus arises from the greater horn (and body) of the hyoid, not the lesser horn.
Chondroglossus, a slip, arises from the lesser horn. (Last's p. 480-4)

questions.s: The lingual nerve in the mouth (Last's):
o: It enters the mouth below the superior constrictor at the lower end of the raphe

The lingual nerve enters the mouth below the lower border of the superior constrictor, at the lower end of the pterygomandibular raphe.
It then lies against the mandible. (Last's p. 480-4)
The submandibular ganglion hangs from it on hyoglossus

The submandibular ganglion hangs from the lingual nerve on the surface of hyoglossus.
Chorda tympani fibres relay there. (Last's p. 480-4)
It lies against the mandible at the second premolar

The lingual nerve lies against the mandible at the posterior border of the third molar, not the second premolar.
That is where it is at risk in extractions. (Last's p. 480-4)
Its gingival branch supplies the buccal gum

The gingival branch of the lingual nerve supplies the lingual gum, not the buccal gum.
The buccal gum is supplied by the buccal and mental nerves. (Last's p. 480-4)
It is about 12 cm long

The pharynx is about 12 cm long, from the skull base to C6.
It lies behind the nose, mouth and larynx. (Last's p. 486-9)
It becomes the oesophagus at C6

The pharynx becomes the oesophagus at the lower border of the cricoid cartilage (C6).
This is the narrowest part of the gut apart from the appendix. (Last's p. 486-9)
The pharyngobasilar fascia attaches to the lateral pterygoid plate

The pharyngobasilar fascia attaches to the medial pterygoid plate, not the lateral plate.
The superior constrictor arises from the medial plate and hamulus. (Last's p. 486-9)
The cartilaginous auditory tube enters below the pharyngobasilar fascia

The cartilaginous auditory tube enters the pharynx above the upper border of the superior constrictor, piercing the pharyngobasilar fascia.
So it lies above, not below, the muscular wall. (Last's p. 486-9)
The middle constrictor arises from the stylohyoid ligament and greater horn

The middle constrictor arises from the angle between the stylohyoid ligament and the greater horn of the hyoid.
It fans out around the pharynx. (Last's p. 486-9)
The internal laryngeal nerve pierces the thyrohyoid membrane between middle and inferior constrictors

The gap between the middle and inferior constrictors is closed by the thyrohyoid membrane, which is pierced by the internal laryngeal nerve and superior laryngeal vessels.
It is a weak point in the pharyngeal wall. (Last's p. 486-9)
The glossopharyngeal nerve passes between middle and inferior constrictors

IX passes between the superior and middle constrictors, with stylopharyngeus.
The internal laryngeal nerve uses the lower gap. (Last's p. 486-9)
The recurrent laryngeal nerve passes deep to the upper border of the inferior constrictor

The recurrent laryngeal nerve passes deep to the lower border of the inferior constrictor, not the upper border.
It enters behind the cricothyroid joint. (Last's p. 486-9)
Palatopharyngeus is the most internal muscle of the wall

Palatopharyngeus lies internal to all the other muscles of the pharyngeal wall.
It forms the palatopharyngeal fold. (Last's p. 486-9)
Stylopharyngeus is supplied by the glossopharyngeal nerve

Stylopharyngeus is the only muscle supplied by IX.
It elevates the pharynx. (Last's p. 486-9)
Salpingopharyngeus arises from the hamulus

Salpingopharyngeus arises from the cartilage of the auditory tube, not the hamulus.
"Salpinx" means tube. (Last's p. 486-9)
The pharyngeal plexus lies mainly over the superior constrictor

The pharyngeal plexus lies mainly over the middle constrictor.
It is formed by IX, X and sympathetic branches. (Last's p. 486-9)
The nasopharynx is supplied by the pharyngeal branch of the pterygopalatine ganglion

The nasopharynx is supplied by the pharyngeal branch of the pterygopalatine ganglion (V2), which runs through the palatovaginal canal.
So nasopharyngeal pain refers to V2 territory. (Last's p. 486-9)
The oropharynx is supplied by the glossopharyngeal nerve

The oropharynx is supplied by IX, the afferent limb of the gag reflex.
Touching the posterior pharyngeal wall triggers it. (Last's p. 486-9)
The tonsillar fossa floor is the middle constrictor

The floor of the tonsillar fossa is the superior constrictor, not the middle constrictor.
IX lies just outside it. (Last's p. 486-9)
The gag reflex efferent is the glossopharyngeal

The afferent limb of the gag reflex is IX; the efferent limb is X.
IX senses, X contracts. (Last's p. 486-9)
It is supplied via the nerve to medial pterygoid

Tensor veli palatini is supplied by V3 via the nerve to medial pterygoid. It is the only palatal muscle not supplied by the pharyngeal plexus.
It is a first-arch muscle. (Last's p. 492-5)
It turns around the hamulus

The tendon of tensor palati turns round the hamulus and spreads out as the palatine aponeurosis.
The hamulus acts as a pulley. (Last's p. 492-5)
It arises from the petrous apex

Levator palati arises from the petrous apex. Tensor arises from the scaphoid fossa, the auditory tube and the spine of the sphenoid.
The two muscles have different origins. (Last's p. 492-5)
It elevates the palate

Tensor palati tenses the soft palate; levator palati elevates it.
Their names describe their actions. (Last's p. 492-5)
It inserts into the nasal surface of the palatine aponeurosis

Levator palati inserts into the nasal (upper) surface of the palatine aponeurosis, between the two heads of palatopharyngeus.
It lifts the palate up and back. (Last's p. 492-5)
It forms a V-shaped sling

The two levators form a V-shaped sling that lifts the soft palate up and back to close the nasopharynx.
Essential for swallowing and speech. (Last's p. 492-5)
It is supplied by the mandibular nerve

Levator palati is supplied by the pharyngeal plexus (X), not the mandibular nerve.
Only tensor is supplied by V3. (Last's p. 492-5)
It arises posterior to the carotid canal

Levator palati arises from the petrous apex in front of (anterior to) the carotid canal, not behind it.
And from the cartilaginous tube. (Last's p. 492-5)
The recurrent laryngeal nerve lies behind the cricothyroid joint

The recurrent laryngeal nerve passes under the inferior constrictor just behind the cricothyroid joint.
The joint is the landmark for finding it. (Last's p. 496-505)
The cricothyroid muscle derives from the 4th arch

Cricothyroid is a fourth-arch muscle, supplied by the external laryngeal nerve.
The other intrinsic muscles are sixth arch (recurrent laryngeal). (Last's p. 496-505)
The superior laryngeal artery arises from the inferior thyroid artery

The superior laryngeal artery arises from the superior thyroid artery.
The inferior laryngeal comes from the inferior thyroid. (Last's p. 496-505)
The inferior laryngeal artery enters through the thyrohyoid membrane

The inferior laryngeal artery enters the larynx with the recurrent nerve under the inferior constrictor. The superior laryngeal artery enters through the thyrohyoid membrane.
Upper vessels through the membrane, lower ones under the constrictor. (Last's p. 496-505)
Laryngeal sensory cell bodies are in the inferior vagal ganglion

Sensory fibres from the larynx have their cell bodies in the inferior (nodose) vagal ganglion.
This applies to both internal and recurrent laryngeal fibres. (Last's p. 496-505)
The recurrent nerve often divides at the upper border of the thyroid isthmus

The recurrent laryngeal nerve often divides into two at the level of the upper border of the thyroid isthmus.
So a surgeon may find two branches. (Last's p. 496-505)
Cricothyroid is supplied by the recurrent laryngeal nerve

Cricothyroid is supplied by the external laryngeal nerve, not the recurrent laryngeal nerve.
It is the only intrinsic muscle not supplied by the recurrent nerve. (Last's p. 496-505)
The internal laryngeal nerve supplies mucosa below the vocal folds

The internal laryngeal nerve supplies the mucosa above the vocal folds. Below them it is the recurrent laryngeal nerve.
The folds divide the two territories. (Last's p. 496-505)
The medial walls of the two orbits are parallel

The medial walls of the two orbits are parallel, while the lateral walls diverge at about 90 degrees to each other.
So each orbital axis points out at about 22.5 degrees. (Last's p. 505-6)
The marginal tubercle of Whitnall is on the zygomatic bone

Whitnall's marginal tubercle on the zygomatic bone gives attachment to the lateral palpebral ligament.
It lies just inside the lateral orbital margin. (Last's p. 505-6)
The inferior orbital fissure lies between greater and lesser wings

The superior orbital fissure lies between the greater and lesser wings of the sphenoid. The inferior fissure lies between the greater wing and the maxilla.
The two fissures form a V. (Last's p. 505-6)
The ethmoidal foramina lie at the junction of medial wall and floor

The ethmoidal foramina lie at the junction of the medial wall and the roof of the orbit (the frontoethmoidal suture).
They are landmarks for the anterior cranial fossa level in orbital surgery. (Last's p. 505-6)
Inferior oblique is the only ocular muscle not arising from the back of the orbit

Inferior oblique arises from the front of the orbital floor; all the other ocular muscles arise at the back of the orbit.
It is the only one with an anterior origin. (Last's p. 508-11)
Lateral rectus has a C-shaped origin across the superior orbital fissure

Lateral rectus arises in a C-shape from the tendinous ring bridging the superior orbital fissure, so it is longer than the other recti.
Structures within the ring pass between its two heads. (Last's p. 508-11)
The superior oblique inserts in front of the equator

Superior oblique inserts behind the equator of the eyeball.
That posterior insertion is why it depresses the adducted eye. (Last's p. 508-11)
The nerve to inferior oblique is the shortest nerve in the orbit

The nerve to inferior oblique is the longest muscular nerve in the orbit.
It runs forward along the floor. (Last's p. 508-11)
It arises from the under surface of the lesser wing

Levator palpebrae superioris arises from the under surface of the lesser wing at the apex of the orbit.
It runs forward above superior rectus. (Last's p. 508-11)
Complete oculomotor palsy causes complete ptosis

A complete III palsy paralyses the striated levator and causes complete ptosis. Sympathetic loss causes only partial ptosis.
Partial ptosis points to Horner's syndrome. (Last's p. 508-11)
Its smooth muscle receives sympathetics from the middle cervical ganglion

The smooth muscle part (superior tarsal muscle) receives sympathetic fibres from the superior cervical ganglion.
They travel via the internal carotid plexus. (Last's p. 508-11)
The frontal nerve lies on its lower surface

The frontal nerve lies on the upper surface of levator, beneath the periosteum of the roof.
It is the first nerve seen when the orbital roof is removed. (Last's p. 508-11)
Seven nerves enter through the superior orbital fissure

Seven nerves enter the orbit through the superior orbital fissure: III (two divisions), IV, VI, and the lacrimal, frontal and nasociliary nerves.
The optic nerve uses the optic canal. (Last's p. 511-12)
The frontal nerve gives no branches to orbital contents

The frontal nerve gives no branches to orbital contents apart from periosteal twigs.
It passes straight through to the forehead. (Last's p. 511-12)
The ciliary ganglion lies medial to the optic nerve

The ciliary ganglion lies lateral to the optic nerve, about a third of the way forward from the apex.
It lies between the nerve and lateral rectus. (Last's p. 511-12)
The optic nerve meets the sclera 3 mm lateral to the posterior pole

The optic nerve meets the sclera about 3 mm medial to (nasal to) the posterior pole.
That is why the optic disc is nasal to the macula. (Last's p. 511-12)

questions.s: The optic nerve in the orbit (Last's):
o: Its orbital length is about 3 cm

The optic nerve is about 3 cm long in the orbit, with slack to allow eye movement.
The straight-line distance is shorter. (Last's p. 511-12)
The ophthalmic artery crosses it from lateral to medial

The ophthalmic artery spirals round the lateral side of the optic nerve and crosses above it from lateral to medial.
The nasociliary nerve crosses with it. (Last's p. 511-12)
The ophthalmic artery crosses it from medial to lateral

The ophthalmic artery crosses the optic nerve from lateral to medial, not medial to lateral.
It started below and lateral in the canal. (Last's p. 511-12)
It lies outside the dural sheath in the orbit

In the orbit the optic nerve lies within its dural and arachnoid sheaths all the way to the back of the eye.
That is why raised pressure is transmitted to the disc. (Last's p. 511-12)
Its secretomotor fibres relay in the pterygopalatine ganglion

Lacrimal secretomotor fibres start in the superior salivary nucleus and travel via the greater petrosal nerve and nerve of the pterygoid canal, relaying in the pterygopalatine ganglion, then via the zygomatic and lacrimal nerves.
A greater petrosal lesion causes a dry eye. (Last's p. 511-12)
The lower eyelid is supplied by the infraorbital nerve

The lower eyelid and its conjunctiva are supplied by palpebral branches of the infraorbital nerve.
Upper lid V1, lower lid V2. (Last's p. 511-12)
Its secretomotor fibres arise in the inferior salivary nucleus

Lacrimal secretomotor fibres arise in the superior salivary nucleus, not the inferior.
The inferior salivary nucleus serves the parotid. (Last's p. 511-12)
The conjunctiva is supplied by a different nerve from the overlying lid

Last's says the conjunctiva is supplied by the same nerve as the overlying lid.
That is why the conjunctival reflex survives loss of the ciliary nerves. (Last's p. 511-12)
