The lacrimal, frontal and trochlear nerves lie outside the cone of muscles

The lacrimal, frontal and trochlear nerves enter lateral to (outside) the tendinous ring and lie outside the muscle cone.
They are safe from intraconal injections. (Last's p. 512-14)
The trochlear nerve enters the upper surface of superior oblique

Last's describes IV sinking into the upper (orbital) surface of superior oblique.
Other ocular motor nerves enter the ocular surfaces of their muscles. (Last's p. 512-14)
The nasociliary nerve lies outside the cone

The nasociliary nerve lies inside the cone, with the divisions of III and VI.
It entered within the tendinous ring. (Last's p. 512-14)
The nerve to medial rectus passes above the optic nerve

The nerve to medial rectus passes below the optic nerve, not above it.
It is a branch of the inferior division of III. (Last's p. 512-14)
Its parasympathetic root comes from the nerve to inferior oblique

Edinger–Westphal fibres reach the ciliary ganglion via the nerve to inferior oblique.
This is its parasympathetic (motor) root. (Last's p. 512-14)
It gives about 12 short ciliary nerves

About 12 short ciliary nerves leave the ganglion and pierce the sclera around the optic nerve.
They carry parasympathetic, sympathetic and sensory fibres. (Last's p. 512-14)
Most postganglionic fibres supply sphincter pupillae

Most postganglionic fibres from the ciliary ganglion supply the ciliary muscle; only about 3 percent supply sphincter pupillae.
Accommodation needs many more fibres than the pupil. (Last's p. 512-14)
Dividing its sensory root abolishes the conjunctival reflex

Last's says dividing the sensory root of the ciliary ganglion abolishes the corneal reflex, not the conjunctival reflex.
The conjunctiva is supplied by lid nerves. (Last's p. 512-14)
The central retinal artery is its first and smallest branch

The central retinal artery is the first and smallest, but most important, branch of the ophthalmic artery. It is an end artery.
Occlusion causes sudden blindness. (Last's p. 512-14)
The central artery enters the inferomedial part of the nerve halfway along

The central retinal artery enters the inferomedial side of the optic nerve about halfway between the optic canal and the eye.
It then runs in the centre of the nerve. (Last's p. 512-14)
Central and posterior ciliary arteries anastomose freely

There is no anastomosis between the central retinal artery and the posterior ciliary arteries.
That is why central retinal occlusion is so damaging. (Last's p. 512-14)
It lies above the optic nerve in the optic canal

In the optic canal the ophthalmic artery lies below and lateral to the nerve, not above it.
It crosses above the nerve later, in the orbit. (Last's p. 512-14)
The superior ophthalmic vein communicates with the angular vein

The superior ophthalmic vein begins above the medial palpebral ligament by joining the angular vein, linking face and cavernous sinus.
This is the route of facial infection into the sinus. (Last's p. 512-14)
The inferior ophthalmic vein drains partly to the pterygoid plexus

The inferior ophthalmic vein drains partly to the pterygoid plexus through the inferior orbital fissure.
The rest joins the superior vein or cavernous sinus. (Last's p. 512-14)
The superior ophthalmic vein drains to the pterygoid plexus

The superior ophthalmic vein drains directly into the cavernous sinus through the superior orbital fissure, not to the pterygoid plexus.
It is the main venous outflow of the orbit. (Last's p. 512-14)
The inferior ophthalmic vein runs above the optic nerve

The inferior ophthalmic vein runs below the optic nerve within the cone; the superior ophthalmic vein runs above it.
Their names match their positions. (Last's p. 512-14)
Superior rectus turns the eye up and in

Because the axis of the orbit is angled outward from the visual axis, superior rectus elevates and adducts the eye (and intorts it).
To test it in isolation, the eye is first abducted. (Last's p. 514-15)
Inferior oblique turns the eye up and out

Inferior oblique elevates and abducts the eye (and extorts it).
It is tested with the eye adducted, looking up. (Last's p. 514-15)
Superior oblique causes extorsion

Superior oblique causes intorsion (with superior rectus). Inferior oblique and inferior rectus cause extorsion.
Superior muscles intort. (Last's p. 514-15)
Inferior rectus turns the eye down and out

Inferior rectus turns the eye down and in (and extorts it).
Superior oblique turns it down and out. (Last's p. 514-15)
The pathway relays in the paramedian pontine reticular formation

The pathway for conjugate horizontal gaze relays in the paramedian pontine reticular formation (Last's para-abducent nucleus), which drives the ipsilateral abducent nucleus.
It is the horizontal gaze centre. (Last's p. 514-15)
Crossed fibres ascend in the medial longitudinal bundle

From the abducent nucleus, crossed fibres ascend in the medial longitudinal bundle to the contralateral oculomotor nucleus (medial rectus subnucleus).
A lesion here causes internuclear ophthalmoplegia. (Last's p. 514-15)
The frontal eye field lies in the inferior frontal gyrus

The frontal eye field lies in the middle frontal gyrus (posterior part), not the inferior frontal gyrus.
Broca's area is in the inferior frontal gyrus. (Last's p. 514-15)
Cold water caloric irrigation induces conjugate deviation to the opposite side

In an unconscious patient with an intact brainstem, ice-cold water in one ear induces conjugate deviation of the eyes towards the same side.
Absence of this response is a brainstem death sign. (Last's p. 514-15)
The sclera is an expansion of the optic nerve dural sheath

The sclera is continuous with the dural sheath of the optic nerve.
It is the tough outer coat of the eye. (Last's p. 516-18)
The ciliary muscle is mesodermal

The ciliary muscle is mesodermal; sphincter and dilator pupillae are ectodermal (from the optic cup).
An unusual origin for smooth muscle. (Last's p. 516-18)
The cornea occupies the anterior third of the globe

The cornea occupies only the anterior sixth of the globe, not the anterior third.
The sclera covers the rest. (Last's p. 516-18)
Descemet's membrane is the anterior limiting layer

Bowman's membrane is the anterior limiting layer of the cornea; Descemet's membrane is the posterior limiting layer.
"B before D" from front to back. (Last's p. 516-18)
The macula lies 3 mm lateral to the optic disc

The macula lies about 3 mm lateral to the optic disc at the posterior pole of the eye.
It contains the fovea. (Last's p. 516-18)
The fovea contains only cones

The fovea contains only cones, giving the sharpest vision.
Rods are absent from its centre. (Last's p. 516-18)
The optic disc is about 5 mm across

The optic disc is about 1.5 mm across, not 5 mm.
It is the blind spot. (Last's p. 516-18)
The ganglion cells lie outermost, next to the pigment epithelium

The ganglion cells lie innermost in the retina, next to the vitreous; light passes through them to reach the receptors.
The rods and cones lie outermost, against the pigment epithelium. (Last's p. 516-18)
The consensual reflex occurs because each pretectal nucleus reaches both Edinger-Westphal nuclei

The consensual light reflex occurs because each pretectal nucleus projects to both Edinger–Westphal nuclei, and partly because of crossing at the chiasma.
So light in one eye constricts both pupils. (Last's p. 518-19)
Accommodation fibres bypass the pretectal nucleus

Accommodation fibres bypass the pretectal nucleus (they come from the cortex), which explains the Argyll Robertson pupil: lost light reflex, preserved accommodation.
A pretectal lesion separates the two. (Last's p. 518-19)
Pupillary fibres run on the ventral surface of the oculomotor nerve near the brainstem

Near the brainstem the pupillary fibres run on the dorsal surface of III, not the ventral surface.
They then move medially and inferiorly along the nerve. (Last's p. 518-19)
Accommodation fibres pass through the posterior limb of the internal capsule

Accommodation fibres from the frontal eye field pass through the anterior limb of the internal capsule, not the posterior limb.
Last's makes this point about the anterior limb. (Last's p. 518-19)
It begins in the posterolateral hypothalamus

The ocular sympathetic pathway begins in the posterolateral hypothalamus and descends through the lateral brainstem to the cord.
Lateral medullary infarction therefore causes Horner's syndrome. (Last's p. 518-19)
Preganglionic neurons are at T1

Preganglionic neurons for the eye are in the lateral horn at T1, leaving in the T1 white ramus.
An apical lung tumour (Pancoast) can damage them. (Last's p. 518-19)
Postganglionic fibres reach the eye mainly via short ciliary nerves

Postganglionic sympathetic fibres reach dilator pupillae mainly via the long ciliary nerves (from the nasociliary nerve), not the short ciliary nerves.
The short ciliary nerves are mainly parasympathetic. (Last's p. 518-19)
Anhidrosis occurs with all Horner's lesions

Anhidrosis of the face occurs only with central or preganglionic lesions. Postganglionic lesions above the carotid bifurcation spare facial sweating, because sudomotor fibres follow the external carotid.
The pattern of anhidrosis helps localise Horner's syndrome. (Last's p. 518-19)
The external acoustic meatus is about 3 cm long

The external acoustic meatus is about 3 cm long: an outer cartilaginous third and an inner bony two-thirds.
It is S-shaped, so the auricle is pulled up and back to straighten it. (Last's p. 523-6)
The deep auricular artery enters through the squamotympanic fissure

The deep auricular branch of the maxillary artery enters the meatus through the squamotympanic fissure.
The anterior tympanic uses the petrotympanic fissure. (Last's p. 523-6)
The extrinsic auricular muscles are supplied by the auriculotemporal nerve

The extrinsic auricular muscles are supplied by the facial nerve (posterior auricular and temporal branches).
The auriculotemporal nerve is sensory. (Last's p. 523-6)
The TMJ is supplied only by the auriculotemporal nerve

The TMJ is supplied by the auriculotemporal nerve and also by the nerve to masseter.
Hilton's law. (Last's p. 523-6)

questions.s: Nerve supply of the external ear (Last's):
o: The great auricular supplies the cranial surface of the auricle

The great auricular nerve (C2, C3) supplies the cranial (back) surface and the lower lateral surface of the auricle.
It also supplies the skin over the parotid. (Last's p. 523-6)
The vagus supplies posterior meatal skin

The auricular branch of the vagus supplies the skin of the posterior part of the meatus and part of the tympanic membrane.
Stimulating it can cause coughing. (Last's p. 523-6)
The auriculotemporal supplies the lower lateral auricle

The auriculotemporal nerve supplies the upper lateral surface of the auricle and most of the meatal skin, not the lower lateral surface.
The lower part is great auricular. (Last's p. 523-6)
The lesser occipital supplies most of the lateral surface

The lesser occipital nerve supplies only a small area at the top of the cranial surface, overlapping.
It is not the main supply of the lateral surface. (Last's p. 523-6)
The promontory is formed by the first turn of the cochlea

The promontory on the medial wall of the middle ear is the bulge of the basal (first) turn of the cochlea.
The tympanic plexus lies on it. (Last's p. 526-8)
The pyramid lies on the posterior wall

The pyramid lies on the posterior wall; the stapedius tendon emerges from its apex.
The chorda tympani enters just lateral to it. (Last's p. 526-8)
The round window lies above and behind the promontory

The round window lies below and behind the promontory. The oval window lies above and behind it.
The stapes footplate fills the oval window. (Last's p. 526-8)
The trochleariform process lies on the lateral wall

The trochleariform process, around which the tensor tympani tendon turns, lies on the medial wall.
It is a landmark above the oval window region. (Last's p. 526-8)
It is about 1 cm across

The tympanic membrane is about 1 cm across.
It is oval and slightly conical. (Last's p. 526-8)
It lies at about 55 degrees to the meatus

The tympanic membrane lies obliquely at about 55 degrees to the meatus, facing laterally, downward and forward.
The anteroinferior part is furthest from the examiner. (Last's p. 526-8)
Its mucosal surface is supplied by the auriculotemporal nerve

The mucosal (inner) surface of the drum is supplied by the tympanic plexus (IX), not the auriculotemporal nerve.
The outer surface is supplied by the auriculotemporal and vagus nerves. (Last's p. 526-8)
The chorda tympani crosses lateral to the neck of the malleus

The chorda tympani crosses medial to the neck of the malleus, under the mucosa.
It lies inside the drum. (Last's p. 526-8)
The stapes derives from the second arch

The stapes derives from second-arch cartilage; the malleus and incus from the first arch.
So stapedius (second arch) is supplied by VII. (Last's p. 528-9)
The anterior ligament of the malleus continues as the sphenomandibular ligament

The anterior ligament of the malleus passes through the squamotympanic (petrotympanic) fissure to the sphenoid spine as the sphenomandibular ligament, both being remnants of Meckel's cartilage.
A first-arch continuity. (Last's p. 528-9)
The incus derives from the second arch

The incus derives from the first arch, with the malleus.
Only the stapes is from the second arch. (Last's p. 528-9)
The anterior limb of the stapes is longer than the posterior

The anterior limb of the stapes is shorter and straighter than the posterior limb.
A small Last's detail. (Last's p. 528-9)
Tensor tympani inserts into the handle of the malleus

The tendon of tensor tympani turns round the processus trochleariformis to insert into the upper part of the handle of the malleus.
It damps vibration of the drum. (Last's p. 528-9)
Stapedius inserts into the neck of the stapes

Stapedius emerges from the pyramid and inserts into the neck of the stapes; it is supplied by VII.
Its paralysis causes hyperacusis. (Last's p. 528-9)
Tensor tympani relays in the otic ganglion

The nerve to tensor tympani passes near (or through) the otic ganglion without relaying; it is a somatic motor nerve.
Only parasympathetic fibres relay in the ganglion. (Last's p. 528-9)
Stapedius lies in the upper semicanal of the musculotubular canal

Tensor tympani lies in the upper semicanal of the musculotubular canal; stapedius lies in the pyramid.
The lower semicanal is the auditory tube. (Last's p. 528-9)

questions.s: The tympanic plexus and lesser petrosal nerve (Last's):
o: The plexus is formed mainly by Jacobsen's nerve

The tympanic plexus on the promontory is formed mainly by Jacobson's nerve, the tympanic branch of IX.
Caroticotympanic sympathetic fibres also join it. (Last's p. 529-31)
The lesser petrosal nerve emerges through a hiatus lateral to the greater petrosal

The lesser petrosal nerve emerges on the floor of the middle fossa through a small hiatus lateral to that of the greater petrosal nerve.
It then passes to foramen ovale or the petrosal foramen. (Last's p. 529-31)
The lesser petrosal nerve leaves through the posterior wall

The lesser petrosal nerve leaves the middle ear through the anterior wall, above the opening of the auditory tube, not the posterior wall.
It then runs through the petrous bone. (Last's p. 529-31)
Sympathetic fibres reach the plexus with the stylomastoid artery

Sympathetic fibres reach the tympanic plexus as the caroticotympanic nerves from the internal carotid plexus, not with the stylomastoid artery.
They pierce the wall of the carotid canal. (Last's p. 529-31)
It is more than 3 cm long

The auditory tube is over 3 cm long: about 1 cm bony and 2 cm cartilaginous.
In children it is shorter and more horizontal. (Last's p. 529-31)
The isthmus lies posteromedial to the sphenoid spine

The narrowest part of the tube (the isthmus), where bone meets cartilage, lies posteromedial to the spine of the sphenoid.
It is the commonest site of obstruction. (Last's p. 529-31)
Its bony part is longer than its cartilaginous part

The cartilaginous part (2 cm) is longer than the bony part (1 cm).
The opposite of the external meatus. (Last's p. 529-31)
Its cartilaginous part is supplied by the tympanic plexus

Last's says the cartilaginous part is supplied by the nervus spinosus; the bony part by the tympanic plexus.
The ostium is supplied by the pharyngeal branch of the pterygopalatine ganglion. (Last's p. 529-31)
It is about 1 cm across

The mastoid antrum is about 1 cm across and is adult-sized at birth.
It is the main air space of the mastoid. (Last's p. 529-31)
It connects to the epitympanic recess by the aditus

The aditus links the epitympanic recess to the antrum. The lateral semicircular canal and the facial canal lie in its medial wall.
Infection spreads backward through it. (Last's p. 529-31)
It lies 5 mm deep to the suprameatal triangle

In the adult the antrum lies about 15 mm deep to the suprameatal triangle, not 5 mm.
In infants it is more superficial. (Last's p. 529-31)
Mastoid air cells develop before birth

The mastoid air cells develop from the first year onward, after birth, as the mastoid process grows.
Only the antrum is present at birth. (Last's p. 529-31)
The cochlea makes 2.75 turns

The cochlea makes about two and three-quarter turns around its central bony pillar, the modiolus.
The basal turn forms the promontory. (Last's p. 531-5)
The scala vestibuli and tympani communicate at the helicotrema

The scala vestibuli and scala tympani communicate at the apex through the helicotrema.
Both contain perilymph. (Last's p. 531-5)
Endolymph and perilymph communicate freely

Endolymph and perilymph do not communicate; they are separate fluids in separate compartments.
Their different compositions are essential for hearing. (Last's p. 531-5)
The perilymphatic duct opens into the internal acoustic meatus

The perilymphatic duct opens into the cochlear canaliculus, which reaches the subarachnoid space at the jugular foramen, not the internal acoustic meatus.
It links perilymph with CSF. (Last's p. 531-5)
The anterior canal produces the arcuate eminence

The anterior (superior) semicircular canal lies across the long axis of the petrous bone and raises the arcuate eminence.
It is a middle fossa landmark. (Last's p. 531-5)
There are five openings into the vestibule

The three semicircular canals open into the vestibule by five openings, because the anterior and posterior canals share a crus commune.
So there are five, not six, openings. (Last's p. 531-5)
The lateral canal opens by a crus commune

The anterior and posterior canals share the crus commune; the lateral canal opens by two separate openings.
The lateral is horizontal. (Last's p. 531-5)
The posterior canal lies perpendicular to the long axis of the petrous bone

The posterior canal lies parallel to the long axis of the petrous bone; the anterior canal lies perpendicular to it.
So each anterior canal is parallel to the opposite posterior canal. (Last's p. 531-5)
The stria vascularis produces endolymph

The stria vascularis on the outer wall of the cochlear duct produces endolymph.
It maintains the endocochlear potential. (Last's p. 531-5)
The saccule lies in the spherical recess

The saccule lies in the spherical recess and the utricle in the elliptical recess of the vestibule.
Saccule and spherical go together. (Last's p. 531-5)
The utricle connects to the cochlear duct by the ductus reuniens

The saccule, not the utricle, connects to the cochlear duct by the ductus reuniens.
The utricle connects to the semicircular ducts. (Last's p. 531-5)
The maculae serve kinetic balance

The maculae (of utricle and saccule) serve static balance; the cristae (in the ampullae) serve kinetic balance.
Maculae detect gravity; cristae detect rotation. (Last's p. 531-5)
The labyrinthine artery usually arises from AICA

Last's says the labyrinthine artery usually arises from AICA, though it may arise directly from the basilar.
It is an end artery. (Last's p. 531-5)
The labyrinthine vein drains to the inferior petrosal sinus

The labyrinthine vein drains to the inferior petrosal sinus.
It accompanies the artery in the internal meatus. (Last's p. 531-5)
The vein of the vestibular aqueduct joins the inferior petrosal sinus

The vein of the vestibular aqueduct joins the superior petrosal sinus; the vein of the cochlear aqueduct joins the inferior petrosal sinus.
Two veins, two sinuses. (Last's p. 531-5)
The stylomastoid artery does not supply the labyrinth

The stylomastoid artery assists in supplying the labyrinth (semicircular canals).
So it does contribute. (Last's p. 531-5)
